name: SpoonJoy
epitaph: Cooked in eight kitchens. Ran out of gas.
oneLiner: A Bengaluru app that cooked meals in its own kitchens and delivered them to offices, on demand or as a weekday subscription.
causeOfDeath: It ran eight kitchens and opened a second city on about $1 million, then could not raise more and stopped cooking within five months of its last round.
moneyNote: Raised figure is the $1 million Series A from SAIF Partners (May 2015); an earlier angel round in late 2014 was undisclosed, so the true total is a little higher. No valuation was published. Grofers' 2015 deal was reported as mostly stock with some cash, at an undisclosed price.
inOneMinute: SpoonJoy doubled to about **700–750 orders a day** in five months, backed by Flipkart's Sachin Bansal and then SAIF Partners.
It ran **eight kitchens** and moved into Delhi on about $1 million, then failed to raise more and stopped cooking in October 2015.
Grofers took the team and closed the food business. The founders later built **Hevo Data**, which raised $43 million.
killerLine: If your model needs kitchens, vans and cooks, **raise for the model you chose**, not for the app you imagine.

chapters.title: The idea
chapters.body: Manish Jethani had already co-founded one startup, a business-to-business reverse-auction site called Vendors Scale. In 2014, in Bengaluru, he started SpoonJoy, later joined by co-founders Sourabh Agarwal, Prateek Agrawal and Kanishk Tyagi. The pitch was simple: busy office workers want a decent lunch without a long wait. SpoonJoy offered **on-demand lunch and dinner** plus a Monday-to-Friday subscription of fruit boxes, salads, sprouts and snacks. You chose the dishes and the time; SpoonJoy did the rest. In December 2014 it was getting **350–400 orders a day**, mostly from offices, and raised angel money from a remarkable group: Flipkart co-founder Sachin Bansal, Flipkart's Mekin Maheshwari, Tracxn's Abhishek Goyal and Delhivery's Sahil Barua.

chapters.title: The rise
chapters.body: By May 2015 orders had roughly doubled to **700–750 a day**. About 90% came from offices and 70% through the mobile app. SpoonJoy promised delivery in 30 minutes. To keep that promise it did not rely on restaurants: it ran **eight of its own kitchens** across Bengaluru, serving areas like Indiranagar, Koramangala, MG Road and HSR Layout. On 1 May it raised $1 million in a Series A from SAIF Partners. The plan was to upgrade its technology and open Delhi and Mumbai within about two months. It was a crowded field, with FreshMenu, Yumist, TinyOwl, Zomato, Foodpanda and Swiggy all chasing the same hungry office crowd.

chapters.title: The cracks
chapters.body: Kitchens are expensive. Each one needs rent, equipment, cooks and supplies before the first order, and SpoonJoy's demand was concentrated in **weekday office lunches**. At first, dinner was offered only in HSR Layout. Food also has thin margins. Jethani later said that **"the data needs to be highly optimized"** in food delivery, because every wasted trip eats the profit. Meanwhile SpoonJoy pushed into Delhi, adding a second set of kitchens and riders. But no new round followed. By October 2015, about five months after its $1 million round, the money had **run out**.

chapters.title: The fall
chapters.body: In early October 2015 SpoonJoy **stopped operating in both Delhi and Bengaluru**. Reports said Grofers, the grocery-delivery startup flush with fresh funding, was in talks to buy it. Within weeks Grofers had acqui-hired SpoonJoy (bought the company mainly to hire its team), in a deal reported as mostly stock with some cash. Grofers said it took on the team but would **discontinue SpoonJoy's food business**, because it had no plans to enter food delivery. The SpoonJoy app went quiet for good. For customers it was one more food app gone in a bad year. For its founders, it was the start of about a year working inside Grofers.

timeline.event: Manish Jethani starts SpoonJoy in Bengaluru, run by Emvito Technologies.
Raises angel money from Sachin Bansal, Mekin Maheshwari, Abhishek Goyal and Sahil Barua; 350–400 orders a day.
Raises a $1 million Series A from SAIF Partners; plans Delhi and Mumbai.
Hits 700–750 orders a day from eight Bengaluru kitchens.
Opens in Delhi, its second city (month not reported).
Runs out of money and stops operating in Delhi and Bengaluru.
Reported to be selling to Grofers.
Grofers acqui-hires the team and discontinues the food business.
Jethani and Agarwal launch Hevo Data with a $1 million seed round.
Hevo raises a $30 million Series B led by Sequoia Capital India.

charts.takeaway: Orders roughly doubled in five months, but five months after that the money was gone. We plot the midpoint of the 350–400 and 700–750 ranges the company gave.

mistakes.title: Built a heavy model on a light wallet
mistakes.explain: SpoonJoy ran **eight kitchens** plus its own delivery, on angel money and a $1 million round. A marketplace app can survive on that; a chain of kitchens usually cannot, because rent, cooks and stock must be paid every month whatever the orders. The model needed either far more money or far fewer kitchens.

mistakes.title: Opened a second city too soon
mistakes.explain: Within months of raising $1 million, SpoonJoy planned Delhi and Mumbai and did open in Delhi. A new city means new kitchens, riders and marketing, with none of Bengaluru's word of mouth. When the money ran out, it had to **shut both cities at once**. Proving Bengaluru could stand alone would have bought time.

mistakes.title: Relied on one busy hour
mistakes.explain: About **90% of orders came from offices**, and dinner was at first offered in just one area. That suggests demand piled up at weekday lunch, while kitchens and staff were paid for all day, every day. This is our reading of the figures, not a company statement, but it is a common trap for office-food startups.

mistakes.title: Fought a crowded field without a war chest
mistakes.explain: FreshMenu, Yumist, TinyOwl, Zomato, Foodpanda and Swiggy were all chasing the same customers in 2015. When SpoonJoy needed more money, none came. With **no reserve to ride out the winter**, a small company has to stop the moment its last cheque runs out.

warningSigns: Does your business need its own kitchens, warehouses or vehicles, but you have raised only app-sized money?
Are you planning a new city while your first one still needs fresh funding to survive?
Does most of your demand arrive in one short window, while your costs run all day?
If no new money came in, would you run out within six months?
Are several much richer rivals chasing exactly the same customers as you?

lessons.title: Match the money to the model
lessons.detail: List what your model must own: kitchens, vans, stock. Price a year of it. If that is far more than you can raise, choose a lighter model, like partnering with existing kitchens, before you start.

lessons.title: Fill the empty hours
lessons.detail: If your kitchen is busy only at lunch, find a second use for it: dinner, snacks, catering or supplying other brands. Idle capacity is cost with no income.

lessons.title: One city, then two
lessons.detail: Make your first city pay its own bills before moving. A second city halves your attention and doubles your fixed costs.

lessons.title: A soft landing protects people
lessons.detail: SpoonJoy's sale to Grofers gave its team jobs instead of an empty office. When the end is near, look for a buyer for your team early, while you still have something to offer.

lessons.title: Turn your worst pain into your next idea
lessons.detail: Jethani and Agarwal struggled to make sense of SpoonJoy's data. That exact problem became Hevo Data. Keep notes on what hurts while you build; one of those pains may be a company.

quote.text: One of the challenges of food delivery is that the data needs to be highly optimized
quote.who: Manish Jethani, SpoonJoy founder, later CEO of Hevo Data
quote.context: Looking back on SpoonJoy in 2017, explaining why thin food margins made every delivery decision matter, as reported by TechCrunch.

afterlife.text: After about a year at Grofers, Manish Jethani and Sourabh Agarwal started Hevo Data in 2017, a tool that pulls a company's data from many apps into one place. The idea came straight from SpoonJoy, where checking why orders rose or fell meant digging through many tools by hand. Hevo raised a $1 million seed round, an $8 million Series A in 2020 and a $30 million Series B led by Sequoia Capital India in December 2021, about $43 million in all, and said it had over 1,000 customers in more than 40 countries.
